This critical narrative review examines how thresholds, pregnancy physiology, clinical periods, target and reference conditions, and intended clinical tasks influence the interpretation of published performance estimates, rather than seeking a universally superior instrument. Methods: Primary studies, guidance, and methodological literature identified by a structured non-systematic search were synthesised narratively. Results: In a period-stratified analysis identified in this review, one pregnancy-adjusted rule detected 57.8% of administratively coded sepsis cases before 20 weeks and 82.8% at 28-36 weeks, at false-positive rates of 6.3% and 6.7% in matched comparison series; physiology may explain this difference, but case mix was not accounted for. Among women with chorioamnionitis or endometritis, five rules (systemic inflammatory response syndrome criteria, two pregnancy-adjusted screens, and two maternal early warning tools) discriminated poorly. Conclusions: The evidence does not establish a universally superior obstetric sepsis screening instrument, nor equivalence between instruments: each estimate describes an instrument under specified conditions. Published estimates should be interpreted for the intended task (screening, diagnostic confirmation or prognostication), and validation studies should report the target condition, reference condition, and clinical period with every estimate.

articles.title: Molecular Nuclear Imaging in Neurodegenerative Disorders: Advances in Amyloid and Tau PET, Dopaminergic Imaging, and Emerging Protein-Specific Tracers, 1992-2025.
articles.abstract: UNLABELLED: Background/Objectives: Molecular nuclear imaging has substantially advanced the diagnosis and monitoring of neurodegenerative disorders over the past three decades, yet no previous evidence synthesis has mapped the full breadth of amyloid, tau, dopaminergic and emerging protein-specific tracer research against a single conceptual framework. This scoping review was undertaken to map the available evidence on molecular nuclear imaging in neurodegenerative disorders between 1 January 1992 and 31 March 2025, to identify the tracer classes studied, the clinical questions addressed, the source-type distribution of the literature, and the research gaps that would inform future systematic reviews or regulatory submissions. Methods: We followed the JBI methodology for scoping reviews and report against the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR 2018). A Population-Concept-Context (PCC) framework was pre-specified. POPULATION: adults with neurodegenerative disorders (Alzheimer's disease and related dementias, Parkinson's disease and related parkinsonisms, dementia with Lewy bodies, atypical tauopathies, multiple system atrophy, frontotemporal lobar degeneration). CONCEPT: molecular nuclear imaging using amyloid, tau, dopaminergic, α-synuclein or TDP-43 tracers. CONTEXT: clinical or clinical-translational applications in humans. Searches were executed in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and Web of Science and supplemented with grey literature. Consistent with scoping-review methodology, primary human clinical studies, systematic and narrative reviews, consensus statements, procedure standards and clinical guidelines were all eligible as sources of evidence. Sources were charted (not extracted) and synthesised through thematic mapping; a formal critical appraisal of individual sources was not conducted, consistent with JBI guidance. Results: Fifty-two sources of evidence were mapped; 43 primary human clinical studies and 9 consensus statements, procedure standards and clinical guidelines. The mapped evidence spans amyloid PET (first demonstrated with 11C-PiB in 2004, succeeded by three 18F-labelled agents with FDA/EMA approval), tau PET (first-generation 18F-flortaucipir with documented off-target binding, and second-generation 18F-MK-6240, 18F-PI-2620, 18F-RO-948, 18F-PM-PBB3 and 18F-GTP1), dopaminergic imaging (123I-ioflupane/FP-CIT SPECT, 18F-FDOPA and 18F-FE-PE2I PET), and emerging α-synuclein tracers in preclinical or early-phase human evaluation (18F-ACI-12589, 18F-F0502B, 11C-MODAG-005 and SPAL-T-06). Three thematic gaps dominate: (i) absence of head-to-head comparative studies between amyloid tracers and between tau tracers, (ii) under-representation of α-synuclein PET at the clinical-validation stage, with no tracer yet approved for routine use, and (iii) scarcity of standardised quantification thresholds for therapeutic monitoring in the anti-amyloid immunotherapy era. Conclusions: The mapped evidence base is methodologically mature for amyloid and tau PET and for dopaminergic imaging, but under-developed for α-synuclein and TDP-43 imaging and for threshold-based therapeutic monitoring. The research-gap matrix proposes four focused systematic-review questions as priorities for the next decade.

articles.title: Bifid and Trifid Mandibular Canals: A Scoping Review of the Classification Systems and Proposal of an Integrated Anatomical Framework.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Accessory mandibular canals are frequent anatomical variations, and failure to recognize them may lead to incomplete anesthesia, bleeding, and neurosensory disturbances. Several systems have been proposed to classify bifid (BMCs) and trifid (TMCs) mandibular canals, but how consistently they are applied in cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) research remains unclear. This scoping review aimed to map CBCT-based classification systems for BMCs and TMCs and to identify anatomical variants not addressed by existing systems. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Embase were searched up to 31 May 2026. Original CBCT studies proposing, modifying, or applying a classification of accessory mandibular canals were included. Two reviewers independently screened records and charted data on the classification adopted, its modifications, and unclassified variants. Results: Sixty studies were included: forty-two applied a classification for BMCs, seventeen focused exclusively on retromolar canals (RMCs), and one on temporal crest canals (TCCs). The system by Naitoh et al. was the most frequently adopted, yet no study applied it without modification; changes included omission of subtypes, buccal/lingual subdivision, and the addition of superior, inferior, and trifid categories. Equivalent inferiorly directed canals were reported under three different names, RMCs and TCCs were classified using independent systems, and only one study proposed a dedicated subclassification for TMCs. Conclusions: CBCT-based classifications of accessory mandibular canals are fragmented and inconsistently applied. A conceptual three-level framework based on branching multiplicity, site of origin, and spatial trajectory is proposed to improve cross-study comparability; its reliability requires validation on independent CBCT datasets.

articles.title: From Bench to Bedside: Clinical Translation of Electrochemical Biosensors for Viral Diagnostics.
articles.abstract: Electrochemical biosensors have emerged as promising platforms for rapid viral diagnostics, offering high analytical sensitivity, portability, short detection times, and potential compatibility with point-of-care testing. Advances in electrode nanostructuring, biorecognition strategies, signal amplification, and miniaturized instrumentation have enabled remarkably low limits of detection, reaching femtomolar and attomolar concentrations for synthetic viral targets under optimized experimental conditions. However, exceptional analytical performance under controlled conditions does not necessarily translate into clinical diagnostic utility. This review examines the progression of electrochemical biosensors from analytical proof-of-concept toward clinical application, emphasizing the evidence required for successful translation. Following a brief overview of viral targets, recognition strategies, and electrochemical detection approaches, particular attention is given to studies evaluating authentic clinical specimens, including those targeting SARS-CoV-2, dengue virus, human papillomavirus, and hepatitis C virus. Despite encouraging findings, clinical validation remains limited by small sample sizes, incomplete reporting of diagnostic sensitivity and specificity, and insufficient multicentre evaluation, while many platforms have been assessed only using artificial or spiked matrices. Additional challenges include matrix interference, biofouling, reproducibility, sample preparation, manufacturing consistency, stability, workflow integration, and regulatory requirements. Importantly, analytical limits of detection must be interpreted in relation to viral biology, specimen characteristics, clinically relevant thresholds, and intended clinical use. Future research should prioritize reproducible sample-to-answer performance over increasingly extreme analytical sensitivity. Accordingly, this review proposes a staged translational framework encompassing native-matrix analytical validation, adequately powered clinical studies, multicentre reproducibility, manufacturing and usability assessments, and regulatory evaluation. Ultimately, the clinical adoption of electrochemical biosensors will depend on robust evidence demonstrating reliable diagnostic performance in real-world healthcare settings.

articles.title: From Diagnostic Imaging to Surgical Management: Patient-Specific Three-Dimensional Modelling in Gynaecological Cancer-A Scoping Review.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Patient-specific three-dimensional (3D) models may clarify complex anatomy in gynaecological cancer surgery. This scoping review mapped applications of virtual and printed models, and examined their reported contributions to surgical planning and outcomes. Methods: The review followed Joanna Briggs Institute guidance along with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews. PubMed, Scopus and Embase were searched on 4 March 2026 for English- or Spanish-language reports. Following a broad gynaecological search, an oncology-focused synthesis examined patient-specific models linked to surgical anatomy or planning. Eligibility assessment and data charting were each performed independently by two reviewers. Findings were synthesised descriptively without formal risk-of-bias appraisal or quantitative pooling. Results: Fourteen studies published between 2016 and 2026 were included: nine evaluated virtual models and five incorporated physical printing. Evidence comprised comparative observational studies, small feasibility or prospective studies, and case reports. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging were the main imaging sources. Applications included tumour mapping, depiction of neural and vascular anatomy, and planning complex or recurrent tumour resections. Some comparative studies reported shorter operative times and lower blood losses, whereas others found improved anatomical assessments without significant perioperative differences. Any additional advantage of printing over virtual visualisation remained uncertain. Interpretation was limited by small samples, heterogeneous methods, subjective evaluations, and one mixed malignant and non-malignant cohort. Conclusions: Patient-specific 3D modelling may assist planning in selected complex gynaecological oncology procedures. Evidence of improved clinical outcomes remains insufficient. Prospective comparative evaluations should establish appropriate indications, and determine whether additional anatomical information produces meaningful patient benefit.

articles.title: Beyond Genomic Alterations: Transcriptomic Profiling of Lineage Plasticity in Metastatic Solid Tumors.
articles.abstract: Lineage plasticity allows tumor cells to shift their differentiation state during metastatic progression and treatment. Genomic profiling identifies driver alterations and clonal relationships but does not fully characterize the lineage programs expressed by metastatic lesions. This review examines the complementary role of transcriptomic profiling and histopathology in assessing changes in tumor identity, with emphasis on colorectal, pancreatic, prostate, and lung cancers. We discuss studies of lineage transformation, intermediate cellular states, and loss of lineage fidelity, and their relationship to metastatic progression and therapeutic resistance. Bulk, single-cell, single-nucleus, and spatial transcriptomic approaches provide information on malignant-cell differentiation, intratumoral heterogeneity, and microenvironmental context. Integrating these findings with morphology, immunohistochemistry, and genomic analysis may support the development of biomarkers that characterize metastatic cell states and identify programs associated with resistance. By synthesizing these findings, this review aims to clarify how RNA profiling may complement genomic and histopathological assessment of metastatic tumor identity. It also explores how lineage-associated programs could inform diagnostic biomarkers and therapeutic strategies, including modification of plastic states or targeting of their acquired dependencies. The review discusses the analytical and clinical evaluation needed to connect these biological findings with the assessment of metastatic biopsies.

articles.title: Preoperative Stromal Tumor-Infiltrating Lymphocytes and Sentinel Lymph Node Metastasis in Breast Cancer: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Stromal tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (sTILs) reflect the local antitumor immune response and have been associated with lower nodal involvement in breast cancer. However, evidence regarding their relationship with sentinel lymph node metastasis (SLNM) and clinical utility remains limited. This review evaluated preoperative sTILs in relation to SLNM and axillary risk stratification. Methods: Following PRISMA guidelines and PROSPERO registration (CRD420261357952), PubMed, Scopus, CENTRAL, and EBSCOhost were searched. Observational studies reporting preoperative sTILs and nodal outcomes were included. Nodal positivity definitions varied, including macrometastases alone or broader categories encompassing micrometastases, with isolated tumor cells reported separately where available. Results: Three retrospective studies involving 841 patients were included. Higher sTIL levels were generally associated with lower nodal involvement, but findings were inconsistent. One study reported an association between sTIL density and SLNM (OR = 0.137, p < 0.001), whereas another found limited discrimination by sTIL density alone (AUC = 0.624; 95% CI: 0.559-0.689). Subtype-specific findings varied across studies and thresholds, with no consistent associations in luminal A and luminal B cancers, while findings in TNBC depended on the cutoff. Another study reported significant associations in HR-positive/HER2-negative and HER2-enriched cancers, but not TNBC. No significant differences in sTIL levels across molecular subtypes were observed in one study. Conclusions: Preoperative sTILs may complement axillary risk stratification but cannot currently identify patients who can safely omit SLNB. Although SOUND and INSEMA support SLNB omission in selected patients and SENOMAC supports ALND de-escalation, sTIL-guided selection requires prospective validation.

articles.title: Ruptured Mycotic Superficial Femoral Artery Aneurysm: A Case Report and Systematic Literature Review.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Superficial femoral artery aneurysms (SFAAs) are rare. Often mycotic in origin, they remain a diagnostic challenge because of a lack of clear symptoms. The authors' objective was to report on one case of a true ruptured mycotic SFAA and perform a systematic literature review of available data. Methods: The patient is a 59-year-old person with diabetes with a previous ipsilateral transmetatarsal amputation and newly discovered SFAA. Because of radiological signs of rupture, an emergency aneurismectomy was performed, and a bypass using a contralateral venous graft was constructed. Microbiological and pathohistological analyses confirmed the presence of a true ruptured mycotic SFAA. The recovery was complicated by wound infection and dehiscence; however, after treatment, the wound healed completely. A systematic literature review was conducted where Pubmed and Scopus were searched. Results: Six studies and seven limbs were identified. Most ruptured mycotic SFAAs were treated with open surgery; however, in recent years, the endovascular approach is becoming more common. Most patients ended treatment without complications. In two cases there were reported complications, namely, graft infection after endovascular stenting and death. Conclusions: The available literature in this review seems to prefer open surgical treatment of SFAAs, and when an infection is suspected, established surgical protocols should be followed. The endovascular approach is a minimally invasive approach that could be utilized in select patients only.

articles.title: A Comparative Perspective on Pentraxins as Next-Generation Inflammatory Biomarkers: Beyond CRP-A Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: C-reactive protein (CRP) remains the most widely used inflammatory biomarker in clinical practice, valued for its assay standardization, low cost, and extensive validation. However, CRP is a systemic, hepatically derived marker that typically peaks 24-48 h after an inflammatory stimulus and does not capture localized, tissue-level inflammatory activity. Pentraxin 3 (PTX3), a long pentraxin produced locally by endothelial cells, macrophages, and other stromal cells, rises within 6-8 h of an inflammatory trigger and may provide complementary, tissue-specific information in selected clinical contexts. This narrative review searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for studies published between January 2014 and March 2026 using combinations of the terms "pentraxin 3," "PTX3," and "C-reactive protein"; 15 studies met the inclusion criteria after a structured screening process. Across the reviewed literature, PTX3 showed an earlier peak and stronger associations with disease severity and mortality than CRP in specific settings, including acute coronary syndrome, sepsis, and selected neurological and pregnancy-related conditions, although the findings were not uniform across all patient subgroups, particularly between sexes. Rather than replacing CRP, PTX3 is best understood as a complementary biomarker whose value is realized within a tiered testing strategy, in which CRP remains the first-line test and PTX3 is reserved for defined high-risk or diagnostically ambiguous scenarios. The wider clinical adoption of PTX3 will require assay standardization; defined reference intervals, including sex-specific ranges; and cost-effectiveness data before it can be incorporated into routine practice.

articles.title: Explainable AI for Acute Ischemic Stroke Neuroimaging: A Critical Review of SHAP and Grad-CAM Applications and Their Methodological Limitations.
articles.abstract: In the triage of acute ischemic stroke (AIS), rapid non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT), computed tomography angiography (CTA), and diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (DWI) guide intravenous thrombolysis and endovascular thrombectomy (EVT). Machine learning and deep learning models have reported high discrimination for ischemic lesion detection, malignant cerebral edema (MCE), and 90-day modified Rankin Scale (mRS) outcomes. However, opaque model architectures hinder clinical interpretation. Materials and Scope: This critical review is based on a structured PubMed/MEDLINE query (1 January 2021 to 15 August 2026). Among 34 candidate records, two were excluded during initial screening, and two were unretrievable, yielding 30 fully appraised primary prediction studies (24 acute-AIS core studies and six adjacent neurovascular models). Eight acute-AIS studies were prioritized for detailed main-text comparison, while the remaining 22 studies were comprehensively retained in supplementary synthesis. All 30 available models underwent dual evaluation: prediction-model risk of bias via PROBAST+AI and an independent eight-dimension XAI validity appraisal. Overall risk of bias was High in 93.3% (28/30; driven primarily by Domain 4, analysis) and Unclear in 6.7% (2/30; Li et al. and Huang H. et al.); no study was rated Low. Multicollinearity and Attribution Sensitivity: In radiomic and hemodynamic modeling, strong dependence among interdependent imaging predictors (e.g., ASPECTS, core infarct volume, Tmax > 6 s hypoperfusion volume, and white matter hyperintensities) complicates feature-level SHAP interpretation. Interventional or other marginal-reference formulations can break the dependence between observed and integrated-out features and may evaluate combinations that are poorly supported by the empirical joint distribution. Consequently, individual-feature attributions may be sensitive to the explainer formulation and background/reference distribution and should not be interpreted as unique biological or causal effects. Coarse Saliency and Modality Bias: Grad-CAM generates spatially coarse attribution maps due to convolutional downsampling, making it susceptible to skull-base CT beam-hardening artifacts and MRI susceptibility artifacts. Furthermore, unimodal Grad-CAM architectures inherently fail to contextualize non-imaging clinical covariates (e.g., baseline NIHSS, onset-to-door time). Validation-stage Discrimination and Calibration: Across multicenter studies, cross-cohort discrimination is heterogeneous rather than uniformly attenuated. Cao et al. showed marked internal-to-external attenuation (AUC 0.918 to 0.755), whereas Huang L. et al. (0.78 to 0.88) and Li et al. (0.84 to 0.86) showed preserved or improved external discrimination. Training/development, internal validation, and independent external-validation stages must be distinguished. Calibration and uncertainty quantification (UQ) require separate evaluation; explanation maps alone do not establish reliable clinical probabilities. XAI must transition from descriptive post hoc visualizations into validated clinical decision support. Safe translation requires explicit reporting and sensitivity analysis of feature-dependence handling, quantitative saliency validation (e.g., lesion-mask intersection-over-union [IoU] or Pointing Game hit rates against expert anatomical segmentations, alongside deletion/insertion fidelity curves), multi-vendor image harmonization, and uncertainty quantification. Grouped or hierarchical attribution may be considered when appropriate to the intended explanatory target.

articles.title: Cardiovascular Assessment of the Athlete's Heart: From Electrocardiography and Multimodality Imaging to Genetic Testing and Shared Decision-Making.
articles.abstract: Sustained athletic training induces structural, functional, and electrical cardiac remodeling, collectively termed the "athlete's heart," which may phenotypically overlap with inherited and acquired cardiomyopathies. Distinguishing benign exercise-induced remodeling from occult heart disease is critical, since diagnostic error in either direction carries meaningful consequences, ranging from unwarranted sports disqualification to failure to identify athletes at risk of exercise-related sudden cardiac death. In this narrative review, based on a PubMed/MEDLINE search of the literature published between 2015 and 2026, we summarize the contemporary cardiovascular assessment of athletes, including electrocardiography, echocardiography with speckle-tracking and myocardial work, exercise testing, cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), cardiac computed tomography, nuclear imaging, genetic testing, detraining, sex-specific considerations, and artificial intelligence (AI). Electrocardiography interpreted according to the International Criteria, echocardiography and, when indicated, CMR form the core of the evaluation, whereas the other tools are complementary and reserved for selected clinical questions. Many proposed numerical cut-offs derive from single cohorts and are not interchangeable across vendors, protocols, sexes, ethnicities, and sporting disciplines, and some athletes remain indeterminate despite comprehensive evaluation. We propose a pragmatic, non-validated stepwise framework that keeps diagnostic classification, arrhythmic risk assessment, and sports eligibility distinct and emphasizes multidisciplinary shared decision-making.

articles.title: Approach to Early Rectal Cancer in 2026: The Emerging Role of Endoscopic Intermuscular Dissection.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: The management of early rectal cancer is increasingly shifting toward organ-preserving strategies aimed at maintaining oncological efficacy while minimizing the morbidity and functional impairment associated with radical surgery. However, endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) may provide inadequate deep vertical margins in lesions with deep submucosal invasion. Endoscopic intermuscular dissection (EID) has recently emerged as a deeper resection technique that may address this therapeutic gap. This review summarizes current approaches to early rectal cancer and critically evaluates the emerging role of EID. Methods: A narrative review was conducted using PubMed and Scopus, including relevant English-language studies available through August 2026. Evidence on early rectal cancer, histopathological risk stratification, pre-resection assessment, surgical and endoscopic local excision techniques, oncological and functional outcomes, and management after non-curative resection was reviewed, with particular emphasis on EID. Recent studies and relevant guidelines were considered alongside earlier landmark publications. As a narrative review, the evidence was selected and synthesized without a systematic review protocol. Results: EID enables dissection between the circular and longitudinal layers of the muscularis propria, providing deeper vertical clearance than ESD while preserving rectal wall integrity. Available studies report en bloc and R0 resection rates of approximately 94-96% and 81-83%, respectively, with encouraging three-year oncological outcomes in selected patients with low- and intermediate-risk deep submucosal invasive cancer. However, current evidence is derived mainly from expert centers and limited cohorts, and uncertainties remain regarding proximal rectal lesions, subsequent completion surgery, and long-term oncological outcomes. Conclusions: EID represents a promising organ-preserving option for selected early rectal cancers with deep submucosal invasion, but should not yet be considered standard practice. In selected cT1N0 rectal lesions with suspected deep submucosal invasion, EID may provide greater vertical clearance when conventional ESD is unlikely to achieve an adequate deep resection margin. Expert optical assessment with virtual chromoendoscopy, pelvic MRI and, when appropriate, endorectal ultrasound (EUS), inform pre-resection staging and patient selection. Careful patient selection and multidisciplinary management remain essential, while prospective multicenter studies with longer follow-up are required to establish its oncological safety, reproducibility, and role in clinical practice.

articles.title: More than a Second Pair of Eyes: Artificial Intelligence Across the Breast Imaging Pathway.
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from stand-alone accuracy studies to prospective deployment across breast screening, risk prediction, multimodal diagnosis, treatment response, and workflow support. The goal of this narrative review is to determine which AI applications have demonstrated clinical benefit, which remain technically promising, and what safeguards are required for implementation. We synthesize randomized trials, prospective cohorts, real-world implementations, external validations, systematic reviews, and guidance identified in PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus through 30 June 2026. In screening, AI-supported mammography can increase cancer detection and reduce reading workload, but effects depend on whether AI is used as concurrent support, an independent reader, triage, or partial autonomy; autonomous workflows may shift work and cost downstream through additional recalls. MASAI met its prespecified noninferiority criterion for interval cancer, but this should not be interpreted as proof of equivalence or mortality benefit. Image-based risk models often discriminate better than density or conventional clinical models, although prospective benefit from AI-guided allocation to supplemental imaging has not yet been demonstrated. Evidence for contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM), MRI, ultrasound, radiomics, and multimodal models is less mature and limited by external validation, domain shift, missing data, operator dependence, and uncertain incremental value beyond clinicopathological factors. Ungrounded large language models and opaque foundation models are not suitable for autonomous clinical advice. Current evidence therefore supports controlled, task-specific integration rather than radiologist replacement; real clinical benefit depends on governance of the whole AI-enabled pathway, including local validation, human factors, downstream resource use, statistical stopping rules, and fallback procedures.

articles.title: OBESUS (OBESity UltraSound): A Multiorgan Bedside Ultrasound Framework for Obesity Phenotyping.
articles.abstract: Obesity is a heterogeneous chronic disease in which cardiometabolic and functional risks are influenced not only by total body fat but also by adipose tissue distribution, ectopic lipid accumulation in non-adipose tissues, and alterations in skeletal muscle composition. Traditional anthropometric measurements, such as body mass index and waist circumference, fail to capture these biological differences. Point-of-care ultrasound provides a portable, radiation-free, repeatable, and widely available bedside tool for assessing multiple adipose and muscular compartments, yet a broadly standardized framework integrating these measurements into a multiorgan obesity phenotype remains lacking. We propose OBESUS (OBESity UltraSound), a pragmatic multiorgan point-of-care ultrasound framework for structured obesity phenotyping. To facilitate competency-based and stepwise implementation, OBESUS comprises two complementary tiers: OBESUS-Core evaluates abdominal subcutaneous adiposity, preperitoneal fat thickness, hepatic steatosis, and rectus femoris muscle echogenicity, whereas OBESUS-Plus incorporates epicardial and perirenal adipose tissue as additional regional adipose tissue depots of cardiorenal relevance. Rather than generating a numerical score, the framework integrates these findings into four non-mutually exclusive ultrasound-derived phenotypes: metabolic, increased muscle echogenicity, epicardial adiposity, and perirenal adiposity. This narrative review describes the conceptual basis, standardized acquisition methodology, pragmatic reference thresholds, and potential clinical applications of OBESUS. The framework is intended to provide a foundation for prospective evaluation of its reproducibility, clinical validity, prognostic significance and potential utility for longitudinal monitoring.

articles.title: Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance for Lifelong Surveillance in Congenital Heart Disease: From Childhood to Adulthood.
articles.abstract: Advances in paediatric cardiology, surgery and catheter intervention have enabled most children with congenital heart disease (CHD) to reach adulthood, yet transfer to adult congenital heart disease (ACHD) care remains a period at risk of discontinuity and of delayed recognition of residual lesions, ventricular dysfunction, arrhythmias and aortopathy. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) provides radiation-free, reproducible assessment of anatomy, ventricular volumes and function, flow, shunts and myocardial tissue. This narrative review examines CMR as a tool for continuous longitudinal surveillance from childhood into adult life. Its role is not to replace echocardiography but to answer questions that echocardiography cannot resolve reliably and to provide serially comparable measurements, particularly after tetralogy of Fallot repair, in systemic right ventricles, in Fontan circulation and in coarctation of the aorta. We describe lesion-specific protocols, standardised phase-contrast acquisition and ventricular contouring that permit valid serial comparison, and the clinical, electrocardiographic, biochemical (NT-proBNP) and echocardiographic triggers that prompt earlier CMR or allow it to be deferred. CMR timing should therefore follow the lesion and the patient's trajectory rather than chronological age, with transfer regarded as one point on a continuous surveillance pathway. Limitations include examination duration, arrhythmia, device artefacts, contrast considerations and limited access to congenital imaging expertise.

articles.title: Serial Echocardiography in Pediatric Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension: A Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: Echocardiography is central to the serial evaluation of children with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), but the evidence supporting each measurement addresses distinct questions: measurement reliability, association with invasive hemodynamics, prediction of clinical events, and change during treatment. Rather than cataloguing imaging techniques, this focused narrative review provides a domain-by-domain evidence map and a practical interpretation framework for follow-up. PubMed-based targeted literature retrieval and citation tracing were used to assemble pediatric reference, method-comparison, hemodynamic validation, prognostic, and longitudinal studies; formal systematic screening or certainty grading was not performed. Evidence is explicitly stratified by PAH-specific versus broader pulmonary hypertension (PH) populations. Tricuspid regurgitation velocity and pulmonary artery acceleration time have important age- and phenotype-dependent limitations. Tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE), fractional area change, strain, ventricular geometry, and atrial indices have differing prognostic support, but direct validation of within-child change remains much more limited. Some treatment cohorts report improvement in right ventricular (RV) functional markers without commensurate changes in estimated pressure, while acute responsiveness does not necessarily predict long-term outcome. We synthesize these findings in a cross-domain table and a proposed stepwise approach that first checks measurement comparability, then reports domain-specific change, and finally integrates symptoms, WHO functional class, NT-proBNP, exercise capacity, and phenotype. The approach is a reporting aid, not a validated risk score or treatment algorithm. Research should prioritize repeat-acquisition reproducibility, the incremental prognostic value of serial change, and external validation.

articles.title: From Detection to Decision: Linking Microbiological Diagnostics to the Clinical Management of Carbapenem-Resistant Acinetobacter baumannii Infection.
articles.abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB) remains a major diagnostic challenge in healthcare-associated infections. Effective management requires clinicians to determine whether a positive result represents active infection, characterize resistance, and identify treatment options. This narrative review examines established and emerging CRAB diagnostic methods, their clinical applications, limitations, and potential to guide antimicrobial therapy. Molecular assays detect selected carbapenem-resistance determinants; however, their target range limits interpretation, and gene detection alone cannot establish the full susceptibility profile. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) remains essential for assessing isolate-specific activity. Method-dependent uncertainty is especially important for agents such as cefiderocol and colistin. Whole-genome sequencing supports resistance analysis, strain characterization, and outbreak investigation. Metagenomic sequencing, CRISPR-based assays, laboratory automation, and artificial intelligence offer additional capabilities, although their role in routine CRAB management is not established. Distinguishing active infection from colonization remains difficult, particularly with respiratory and wound specimens. Evidence that rapid diagnostic pathways improve outcomes specifically in CRAB infection remains limited; findings from broader bloodstream-infection populations cannot be generalized to every CRAB presentation. Future multicenter studies should validate integrated diagnostic-management pathways and assess their effects on treatment decisions and patient outcomes. Integrating clinical assessment with reliable organism identification and susceptibility testing can support timely, targeted treatment while minimizing unnecessary antimicrobial exposure when CRAB detection represents colonization without evidence of active infection.

articles.title: Urinary Biomarkers of Renal Involvement in Antineutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibody (ANCA)-Associated Vasculitis: Diagnosis, Disease Activity and Relapse Prediction.
articles.abstract: Kidney involvement largely determines prognosis in antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis (AAV), yet serum creatinine, proteinuria and haematuria cannot reliably separate active vasculitis from chronic damage or flare mimics, and kidney biopsy is invasive and rarely repeated. Unlike recent systematic reviews, which assessed a few soluble serum and urinary markers of overall disease activity, this structured narrative review covers the full range of urinary markers of renal involvement, organises them by clinical question and grades the evidence for each. A PubMed search identified 77 clinical studies. Urinary soluble CD163 is the most extensively validated marker; an accredited assay identified renal flare with an area under the curve of 0.95 in a prospective multicentre cohort. Urinary CD4+ T cells discriminate active glomerulonephritis and, in one prospective study, predicted six-month renal relapse with high specificity but modest sensitivity. Persistent haematuria after induction is the most consistently replicated predictor of renal relapse, whereas persistent proteinuria or albuminuria mainly predicts kidney failure. Urinary MCP-1 supports within-patient monitoring, and complement fragments and markers of tubular injury and fibrosis mainly add prognostic information. No urinary marker is yet ready for routine use, and the validation needed is outlined.

articles.title: Ergonomics in Facial Ultrasound: Potential Influence on Image Quality, Reproducibility, and Ultrasound-Guided Aesthetic Procedures.
articles.abstract: Ergonomically unfavorable postures remain a major risk factor for work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WRMSDs) among ultrasound operators. Dermatologic and facial ultrasound presents specific ergonomic challenges because it requires delicate transducer manipulation and prolonged static postures. This narrative review examines key ergonomic strategies for dermatologic and facial ultrasound, integrating findings from recent kinematic and occupational studies to promote sustainable, high-quality ultrasound practice. Important considerations include probe handling, scanning technique, patient positioning, and operator posture. Technical innovations, including portable systems, footswitches, and hands-free controls, are discussed, together with education, awareness, training, and future directions. A practical ergonomic workflow for facial ultrasound is also presented. Standardization of patient positioning, ultrasound-system layout, and operator ergonomics is essential for achieving reproducible diagnostic quality while safeguarding practitioner health. Although direct prospective clinical trials specifically addressing facial ultrasound ergonomics remain limited, translating evidence from general ultrasound and interventional practices provides a practical framework for clinical optimization.

articles.title: Topical Therapy for Keratinocyte Carcinoma-Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis of Efficacy and Patient Follow-Up Using Non-Invasive Imaging Techniques.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Topical therapies, primarily imiquimod (IMQ) and 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), have emerged as valuable treatment options in non-melanoma skin cancers (NMSC) due to their facile administration and minimal systemic reactions, especially for patients who are poor surgical candidates. This systematic review evaluates the clinical and histologic clearance rates, recurrence rates as well as the utility of non-invasive imaging modalities in the diagnosis and monitoring of basal cell carcinomas (BCC) and cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Methods: The systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science and Scopus to identify studies assessing the efficacy of topical therapies in BCC and SCC by clinical examination, histopathologic analysis or non-invasive imaging techniques. Articles in which at least ten lesions were evaluated were included. Risk of bias was assessed using validated tools adapted to study design. A network meta-analysis was performed on trials which provided at least one within-trial comparison. Results: Seventy-eight papers encompassing 5066 BCC and 1081 SCC were included in our analysis. The network meta-analysis was constructed from 14 trials, comprising 1633 lesions, 17 treatment nodes, 57 direct treatment comparisons and 12 designs. Favorable clearance rates were reported not only in superficial BCC (sBCC) and Bowen's disease (BD), but also in nodular BCC (nBCC) and invasive SCC (invSCC), suggesting that these therapies may be an effective approach in selected patients with aggressive tumors. Relapse rates remain higher than after surgical excision, highlighting the need for patient follow-up. Reflectance confocal microscopy (RCM) and optical coherence tomography (OCT) improved the detection of recurrent and relapsed tumors in comparison to clinical and dermoscopic examination alone and correlated significantly with histopathological findings, proving that these modalities can contribute significantly to diagnosis and monitoring. Conclusions: Our systematic review demonstrates the efficacy of topical therapies, especially IMQ and 5-FU, in selected cases of sBCC and BD. Results should, however, be interpreted with caution, given the small number of studies included in the network and the heterogeneity of treatment regimens.

articles.title: Imaging the Vascular Component of Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma: From Pathophysiology to Novel Hemodynamic Biomarkers.
articles.abstract: Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide. Intraocular pressure (IOP) is its only validated therapeutic target, yet some patients progress despite controlled IOP, sustaining interest in a vascular contribution. This narrative review summarizes the anatomy and autoregulation of the optic nerve head circulation, the evidence linking low ocular perfusion pressure, impaired autoregulation and endothelial dysfunction to POAG, and the imaging modalities used to assess ocular hemodynamics. Color Doppler imaging consistently shows reduced retrobulbar flow velocities, particularly end-diastolic, and increased resistive indices, whereas OCT angiography shows reduced peripapillary and macular vessel density correlated with structural and functional damage. However, most evidence is cross-sectional and associative, and cannot establish whether hypoperfusion causes or follows retinal ganglion cell loss. No hemodynamic biomarker has been validated for clinical decision-making, and evidence of prognostic value beyond conventional structural and functional assessment remains inconsistent. Laser Doppler holography, a contactless technique providing pulsatile retinal blood flow waveforms, is presented as an emerging tool whose glaucoma-specific evidence is currently limited to a pilot study of four eyes. Vascular biomarkers therefore remain research tools pending standardized acquisition, normative databases and longitudinal validation.

articles.title: Which Definition Is the Gold Standard? Reference-Standard Choice and the Reported Accuracy of Periprosthetic Joint Infection Diagnostic Tests: A Meta-Epidemiological Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) has no gold standard. Accuracy studies borrow one of several composite definitions instead, and these definitions do not label the same patients as infected. We asked how often accuracy studies say which definition they used, and how far the choice moves the numbers they report. Methods: In this systematic review, we searched PubMed on 20 October 2026 for primary accuracy studies of PJI tests and classified each abstract by the reference definition it named. Studies that applied two or more definitions (MSIS 2011/2013, ICM 2018, IDSA 2013, EBJIS proposed or 2021) to the same cohort were assessed further, and accuracy was extracted per definition. Ratios of PJI cases and the change in sensitivity of the alpha-defensin test were pooled with random-effects models. Results: Of 1744 accuracy studies, 437 (25%) named a reference definition in the abstract. The share rose from none before 2012 to 35% from 2021 onward. Seventeen studies reported accuracy under more than one definition in the same patients. EBJIS classified 1.47 times as many patients as infected as MSIS (95% CI 1.33-1.62; 6 cohorts; I2 = 4%) and 1.26 times as many as ICM 2018 (1.08-1.46; 6 cohorts; I2 = 58%). The pooled sensitivity of the alpha-defensin test was 85.6% (76.9-91.4) against MSIS and 56.3% (48.6-63.7) against EBJIS in the same three cohorts, while specificity stayed between 89% and 100%. Across 13 test-cohort pairs, the median change in sensitivity when the reference moved to EBJIS was -18.5 percentage points (IQR -29.0 to -4.9); sensitivity fell in 10 pairs and changed by less than 3 points in three. Conclusions: For several PJI tests, the reported sensitivity depends substantially on the reference definition chosen. A definition that labels more patients as infected is not, for that reason, a more accurate one. Accuracy figures obtained under different definitions should not be pooled or compared as if they measured the same thing, and every accuracy study should name its reference definition in the abstract.

articles.title: Wearable- and Vision-Based Gait Models for Predicting Future Falls in Older Adults: A Systematic Review of Performance, Validation, and Clinical Readiness.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: We reviewed the performance, validation and clinical readiness of wearable- and vision-based models predicting future falls. Methods: Nine databases and supplementary sources were searched for reports published in 2000-20 July 2026 (retrospective PROSPERO registration: CRD420261502037). Eligible populations had a minimum, mean or median age ≥60 years or separable older-adult results. Screening, extraction and appraisal used single-reviewer assessment with second-reviewer verification, rather than independent duplication. Ten of 47 reports (21.28%) lacked complete-article access. Cohort families were synthesized without meta-analysis; PROBAST+AI appraisal was restricted to complete articles. Results: The 47 reports represented 37 cohort families (15-1705 participants; horizons 7 days-5 years). Representative AUCs ranged from 0.51 to 0.99 across 26 families; 24 estimates were apparent, internally validated or validation-unverified. The only independent-cohort evaluation of published models yielded AUCs of 0.49-0.59. Retained domain-level appraisals classified all 37 complete-article evaluations as high risk of bias. Calibration intercept and slope appeared in one report (2.13%); none reported decision curve analysis, net benefit or clinical impact. Conclusions: Interpretability is limited by high risk of bias, sparse events, limited independent validation and missing calibration. The evidence does not support routine deployment; this concerns evidentiary readiness rather than technical potential. Funding: King Salman Center for Disability Research.

articles.title: Diagnostic Performance of Data-Driven MRI Habitat Analysis for Preoperative Prediction of IDH Status in Adult Gliomas: A Systematic Review and Diagnostic Accuracy Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) status is important for the classification and prognosis of adult gliomas. Whole-tumor MRI summary measures may obscure intratumoral spatial heterogeneity, whereas data-driven habitat analysis identifies imaging-defined tumor subregions and may better capture this heterogeneity. This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of MRI habitat analysis for preoperative prediction of IDH status. Methods: We searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), and Wanfang Data from database inception through 22 August 2026. Eligible studies used data-driven MRI habitat analysis to predict IDH status in adult gliomas. Risk of bias was assessed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2) tool. Sensitivity and specificity were pooled using a bivariate random-effects model. We also performed sensitivity analyses, univariable meta-regression, subgroup analyses, and Radiomics Quality Score 2.0 (RQS 2.0) assessment. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261489645). Results: Eighteen reports were included in the systematic review, and 13 independent studies involving 1236 patients contributed to the meta-analysis. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were 0.78 (95% CI, 0.70-0.84) and 0.85 (95% CI, 0.79-0.89), respectively, with an SROC AUC of 0.89 (95% CI, 0.86-0.91). I2 was 82.1% for sensitivity and 71.3% for specificity. Excluding two studies with approximately reconstructed 2 × 2 tables did not materially change the pooled estimates. Radiomics studies and studies using ≥4 habitats showed higher specificity and lower sensitivity, but their overlap limited separate interpretation of feature type and habitat number. Conclusions: MRI habitat analysis showed promising diagnostic performance for preoperative prediction of IDH status in adult gliomas. However, limited external validation and incomplete assessment of reproducibility and clinical utility remain barriers to clinical translation. Future prospective multicenter studies should further evaluate habitat stability, model calibration, and clinical net benefit.

articles.title: Beyond Bronchospasm: Cardiovascular Involvement in Severe Asthma.
articles.abstract: Background: Severe asthma and cardiovascular disease can coexist, mimic one another, and interact through respiratory mechanics and treatment. This narrative review examines these relationships and their implications for intensive care. Main findings: Conventional and tissue Doppler studies identified cardiac abnormalities in asthma before widespread use of speckle tracking in this field. Subsequent deformation studies include predominantly pediatric or non-ICU populations, alongside limited adult acute severe-asthma evidence. Their findings are heterogeneous and largely observational. During exacerbations, dynamic hyperinflation, intrinsic positive end-expiratory pressure, pleural-pressure swings, right-ventricular loading, ventricular interdependence, gas-exchange abnormalities, adrenergic stimulation, and ventilation may alter filling and forward flow without primary cardiomyopathy. Conversely, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction can present with wheezing, but neither B-lines nor an isolated echocardiographic filling index establishes that diagnosis. Four ICU scenarios illustrate low flow despite high ejection fraction, post-intubation shock, congestion with preserved ejection fraction, and arrhythmia with transient dysfunction. Strain may help characterize serial changes but is load dependent; its incremental clinical value in adult ICU asthma remains unestablished. Systemic inflammatory and catecholaminergic pathways may contribute to myocardial vulnerability. Associations involving allergic inflammation and biologic exposure are hypothesis-generating, and do not demonstrate endotype-specific myocardial injury or cardioprotection. Systemic corticosteroids and biologics require separate consideration of respiratory benefit and cardiovascular effects. Conclusions: Severe asthma can be viewed as an unplanned cardiovascular stress test. Integrated assessment of respiratory mechanics, perfusion, rhythm, congestion, and cardiac function should guide care. Persistent abnormalities warrant reassessment for alternative or coexisting disease rather than an automatic diagnosis of asthma-related cardiomyopathy.

articles.title: Practical Application of EndoFLIP in the Evaluation of Patients with Dysphagia.
articles.abstract: Dysphagia evaluation traditionally proceeds from a history and upper endoscopy to high-resolution manometry (HRM), the reference standard for esophageal motor assessment; however, HRM is swallow-dependent, technically demanding, and yields inconclusive or discordant findings, particularly esophagogastric junction outflow obstruction (EGJOO) patterns, in a clinically meaningful proportion of studies. Functional lumen imaging probe (FLIP) Panometry was developed to complement HRM by using impedance planimetry to characterize esophagogastric junction (EGJ) opening and distension-induced esophageal body contractility during sedated endoscopy, offering a mechanical rather than purely pressure-based assessment of esophageal motor function. This review synthesizes the technique, standardized interpretive framework, and clinical evidence supporting FLIP Panometry across the dysphagia evaluation pathway. We describe the FLIP protocol and core metrics, the EGJ distensibility index, maximum EGJ diameter, contractile response pattern, and distensibility plateau that together generate a motility classification per the Dallas Consensus. We then detail FLIP's principal clinical applications: clarifying inconclusive or discordant HRM, particularly EGJOO; providing complementary information at index endoscopy, where integration with endoscopic findings, such as the endoscopic CARS score, can expedite diagnosis and reduce reliance on subsequent HRM; serving as a physiologic outcome measure after achalasia-directed therapy; and characterizing fibrostenotic remodeling in eosinophilic esophagitis through esophageal body distensibility. FLIP's safety profile, interrater reliability, and key limitations, including reduced sensitivity for spastic motor disorders relative to HRM, are reviewed, alongside emerging directions. Taken together, FLIP Panometry has become an established component of contemporary esophageal evaluation, providing mechanistic information that complements, rather than replaces, endoscopy, histology, barium radiology, and manometry in the comprehensive work-up of dysphagia.

articles.title: Cadaveric Research for Understanding Mechanisms and Advancing Diagnosis and Treatment of Osteoarthritis: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Osteoarthritis (OA) mechanisms are extensively investigated to enable the development of improved diagnostics and therapeutic strategies. Cadaveric tissues are frequently used as "healthy" comparators in mechanistic studies and as laboratory models for the development of new surgical techniques and biomechanical studies. In parallel, advanced cell-based therapies for OA are emerging; however, their usage remains limited, particularly because of the restricted availability and variability of living donor tissues. This review evaluates the contribution of cadaveric tissues to our understanding of OA pathogenesis, diagnosis, and treatment development. Methods: A PRISMA-compliant literature search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus. Studies involving cadaveric human tissues in OA research were included; animal studies, reviews, and clinical studies without cadaveric samples were excluded. Results: A total of 120 records were identified, of which 52 met the inclusion criteria. Most studies (n = 22) used cadaveric tissues to investigate mechanisms of joint degeneration and OA pathophysiology. The remaining studies were distributed between the development or optimization of diagnostic techniques (n = 9) and orthopedic or related therapeutic approaches (n = 21). Studies exploring cellular therapies derived from cadaveric tissues were scarce and were predominantly identified through citation tracking and reference list screening. Conclusions: Cadaveric studies have contributed to OA research, particularly in the elucidation of its mechanisms. Their potential in the development of cadaveric-derived cellular therapies for regenerative medicine is still in a preliminary phase of development and analysis. Future research should prioritize standardization and optimization of such approaches for eventual clinical applications.

articles.title: Preoperative Assessment of Solid Pancreatic Lesions Associated with Chronic Pancreatitis.
articles.abstract: Distinguishing solid pancreatic lesions arising in the background of chronic pancreatitis represents an important diagnostic challenge because mass-forming inflammatory lesions and pancreatic cancer share overlapping clinical, serological, and radiological features and their discrimination might delay the curative treatment. The features of chronic pancreatitis such as fibrosis, calcifications with acoustic shadowing, parenchymal atrophy, and main pancreatic duct abnormalities, may either mimic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma or obscure small malignant lesions, thereby limiting the performance of conventional imaging modalities. Surveillance for pancreatic cancer in chronic pancreatitis is recommended only for selected high-risk patients with hereditary pancreatitis; however, in patients with non-hereditary chronic pancreatitis, clinical vigilance for red flags (new-onset diabetes, weight loss, jaundice, rising CA19-9) should prompt urgent imaging diagnosis and tissue acquisition. This review summarizes the current evidence on the diagnostic preoperative assessment of solid pancreatic lesions in chronic pancreatitis, highlighting the roles of computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, endoscopic ultrasound, and histopathological assessment. Endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle biopsy (EUS-FNB) has become the preferred method for tissue diagnosis because of its superior ability to obtain histological core specimens, although the tumors may present low cellularity and the correct targeting is often difficult. False-negative results, or misinterpretation of well-differentiated carcinoma as a benign condition remain real concerns because they delay the appropriate treatment. For these reasons a non-diagnostic biopsy should be interpreted cautiously by a multidisciplinary team especially when the suspicion for cancer is high.

articles.title: HPV16/18 Genotype and Histologic High-Grade Disease in Women with ASC-H Cytology: A Systematic Review of Genotype-Stratified Outcomes.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Human papillomavirus (HPV) genotyping may stratify histologic risk among women with atypical squamous cells that cannot exclude high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (ASC-H). We evaluated genotype-specific high-grade outcomes. Methods: PubMed and Europe PMC were searched on 1 October 2026 and updated on 7 October 2026. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted, and appraised studies in accordance with PRISMA 2020. Eligible English language studies provided ASC-H-specific histologic outcomes for HPV16/18-defined and comparator groups. Risk of bias was appraised with an adapted QUADAS-2 framework (the protocol-specified Joanna Briggs Institute prevalence checklist is reported in an appendix), and certainty was rated with GRADE. An exploratory restricted meta-analysis compared HPV16/18 with other high-risk HPV (hrHPV) for CIN2+/HSIL+ using random effects and modified Hartung-Knapp confidence intervals. Results: Sixteen studies in 17 reports were included; six contributed 1655 women to the restricted comparison. The pooled risk ratio was 1.19 (95% confidence interval, 0.94-1.49), with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 64.9%) and a prediction interval of 0.70-2.01. The results varied with study selection and genotype definition. In four studies with at least 30 hrHPV-negative women, high-grade outcomes occurred in 6.8-18.4%, and HPV-negative carcinomas were reported. Leave-one-out, screening context, and verification-restricted analyses did not show a consistent difference (histology in all participants: RR 1.01, 0.63-1.62). Incomplete verification, confounding by age and screening context, heterogeneous assays and populations, and inaccessible reports limited confidence; certainty was very low for both outcomes. Conclusions: A modest relative difference between HPV16/18 and other hrHPV types cannot be excluded, but the pooled evidence does not demonstrate a consistent incremental risk difference. Other hrHPV types and negative hrHPV results do not exclude high-grade disease. These findings are consistent with current guidance for colposcopic evaluation of all ASC-H without genotype-based deferral.

articles.title: Association Between Lateral-Incisor Morphology and Palatally Impacted Maxillary Canines: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: Maxillary lateral-incisor morphological variations have been associated with palatal maxillary canine impaction, although the nature and strength of this association remain unclear. Aims: To systematically evaluate and quantitatively synthesize the association between maxillary lateral-incisor morphology and palatal maxillary canine impaction. Materials and Methods: Four electronic databases were searched through April 2026 for observational studies comparing lateral-incisor morphology in patients with palatally impacted canines with external controls and/or contralateral non-impacted sides. Risk of bias was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed for sufficiently comparable external-control outcomes. Results: Thirty-five reports representing 34 studies were included, with 19 studies contributing to meta-analysis. Compared with external controls, lateral incisors in patients with palatal canine impaction were significantly narrower mesiodistally (MD -0.40 mm; 95% CI -0.51 to -0.29) and buccolingually (MD -0.53 mm; 95% CI -0.82 to -0.24). Peg-shaped lateral incisors showed the strongest association (OR 6.59; 95% CI 3.85-11.29), whereas root length did not differ significantly (MD -0.21 mm; 95% CI -0.58 to 0.16). Within-person comparisons showed little consistent difference in crown dimensions between affected and contralateral sides, although shorter roots and lower tooth volumes were more frequently observed adjacent to impacted canines. Conclusions: Palatal maxillary canine impaction is associated with smaller and more frequently peg-shaped lateral incisors. The greater differences observed between affected individuals and external controls, compared with those observed between sides within the same individual, suggest a broader developmental phenotype, although local interactions cannot be excluded. Lateral-incisor morphology may therefore serve as a clinical marker of increased susceptibility rather than an isolated diagnostic feature.

articles.title: Anatomical Validity of MRI-Based Choroid Plexus Segmentation: Regional Boundaries, Age-Related Morphology, and Implications for Neuroimaging Biomarkers.
articles.abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived choroid plexus (ChP) volume is increasingly investigated in studies of brain aging and neurodegeneration, yet its anatomical meaning remains uncertain because segmentation methods differ in ventricular coverage, image contrast, and reference annotations. This narrative review examines the anatomical basis and methodological validity of ChP volumetry by integrating evidence on ventricular anatomy, age-related tissue changes, manual and automated segmentation, and associations with cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease. The lateral ventricular ChP, particularly the atrial glomus, is generally easier to delineate on conventional MRI than its thin extensions and the third and fourth ventricular components. Segmentation performance depends on the anatomical reference and acquisition protocol; agreement with manually drawn masks does not necessarily establish complete anatomical coverage. In addition, age-related vascular remodeling, changes in stromal composition, calcification, and cystic alterations can affect MRI appearance and the interpretation of total volume. Although ChP enlargement has been associated with aging, cognitive impairment, and Alzheimer's disease, volume alone cannot identify the contributing tissue compartments or establish blood-cerebrospinal fluid barrier dysfunction. We propose an anatomy-centered approach to ChP volumetry based on explicit regional definitions, complementary measures of spatial and volumetric accuracy, assessment of test-retest and multicenter reliability, and independent biological validation when functional interpretations are intended.

articles.title: Prosthodontic Identification in Forensic Diagnostics: From Conventional Marking to Digital Traceability and AI-Assisted Recognition-A Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: Human identification is a central component of medico-legal investigations and disaster victim identification (DVI), particularly when remains are decomposed, burned, fragmented, or skeletonized. Dental tissues, restorations, and prosthetic appliances may preserve patient-specific information under conditions that compromise other identifying features. This narrative review aimed to examine conventional and digital prosthodontic identification and traceability approaches and to evaluate their potential applications in forensic diagnostics and human identification. A structured search of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar identified publications from January 2000 to August 2026 on prosthodontic identification, digital traceability, AI-assisted implant recognition, blockchain-based dental data management, and complementary oral biometric methods. Records were independently screened by two authors according to predefined eligibility criteria. Of the 1446 records identified, 558 duplicates were removed, and 92 studies were included in the final narrative synthesis. The evidence was synthesized thematically according to the identification or traceability approach. Conventional methods remain simple and accessible but show variable durability and readability, whereas digital and electronic systems offer greater information capacity and retrievability but are limited by technical requirements and incomplete forensic validation. In a 20 min thermal-exposure experiment, acrylic resin blocks were largely destroyed at 800 °C, whereas some metallic identification labels remained readable at 800-1000 °C, with material-dependent differences in preservation and readability among metallic labels at 1200 °C. These findings represent study-specific observations rather than universal thermal resistance thresholds. Digital imaging, intraoral scanning, CAD/CAM records, AI-assisted implant recognition, and blockchain-supported systems further expand traceability, although the overall evidence remains heterogeneous. Prosthodontic identification and traceability encompass complementary conventional and digital approaches rather than a single universally applicable method, while oral biometrics serve only as adjunctive evidence and cannot independently establish identity. Their forensic value depends on durability, retrievability, availability of corresponding antemortem information, interoperability, and appropriate management of sensitive patient data. Further standardized and clinically relevant validation is needed before advanced traceability systems can be routinely incorporated into forensic identification workflows.

articles.title: Gut Microbiota-Derived Biomarkers for the Non-Invasive Detection of Colorectal Cancer and Adenoma: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Gut microbiota dysbiosis is increasingly implicated in colorectal carcinogenesis, and microbial signatures are emerging as non-invasive diagnostic tools. This systematic review synthesised human studies that evaluated gut microbiota composition, microbiota-derived metabolites and microbial biomarkers for the detection of colorectal cancer (CRC) and colorectal adenoma. Methods: Following the PRISMA 2020 statement, PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and the Cochrane Library were searched for studies published between 2015 and 2025, supplemented by Google Scholar and reference-list screening. Human observational and interventional studies reporting microbiota-based diagnostic or associative endpoints were eligible. Data were synthesised narratively, and risk of bias was appraised with QUADAS-2; the protocol was not prospectively registered. Results: Ten studies (5318 participants; nine from East Asia, one from Europe) were included. Four used targeted quantitative PCR, three 16S rRNA sequencing and three shotgun metagenomics, all three combined with metabolomics. Fusobacterium nucleatum and Parvimonas micra were the taxa most frequently enriched in neoplasia (five studies each), together with Peptostreptococcus species, whereas butyrate-producing commensals (Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Roseburia spp.) were depleted. Multi-omics panels achieved the highest discrimination for CRC (area under the curve [AUC] 0.92-0.994), while performance for adenoma was lower (AUC 0.64-0.91). Adding bacterial markers to the faecal immunochemical test (FIT) increased sensitivity for CRC and advanced adenoma at the cost of specificity. Most studies had a high or unclear risk of bias in the patient-selection and index-test domains, and only two evaluated a screening or mixed symptomatic population. No study reported microbial markers separately for the right colon, left colon and rectum, or for early-onset (<50 years) CRC, and age was often unbalanced between cases and controls. Conclusions: Microbiota-derived biomarkers show reproducible associations with colorectal neoplasia and promising diagnostic accuracy, particularly as adjuncts to FIT, but the evidence derives mainly from small, hospital-based case-control studies in East Asian populations, and accuracy for adenomas remains limited. Site-specific and early-onset data are lacking. Standardised, prospective, multi-ethnic validation studies are required before clinical implementation.

articles.title: Cytology of HPV-Independent Cervical Carcinomas: Morphologic Spectrum, Clinical Correlates, and Ancillary Testing.
articles.abstract: Cervical cancer is one of the most common cancers that can be diagnosed by cytologic features. While the past focus was mostly on human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated cervical carcinomas, the studies on HPV-independent cervical carcinomas have become more extensive with the advancement in ancillary tests, including molecular tests. The development of digital pathology also provides additional opportunities for more accurate cytologic diagnosis. We would like to summarise the current knowledge on the epidemiology, cytomorphology, and ancillary studies for different types of HPV-independent cervical carcinomas, and explore the use of digital pathology in the diagnosis of HPV-independent cervical carcinomas. Case reports, case series, and research articles are identified on PubMed using keywords "HPV-independent", "cervical carcinomas", "digital pathology", and the specific names of subtypes of HPV-independent cervical carcinomas. The studies are selected based on their relevance to cytology, with an emphasis on new updates of ancillary tests. HPV-independent cervical carcinomas are classified based on the histological features, with distinct cytomorphological, immunocytochemical, and molecular features for each subtype. The prognosis is generally worse than HPV-associated cervical carcinomas. Accurate diagnosis is limited by a small number of cases and limited exposure among cytotechnicians and cytopathologists. The use of digital pathology can potentially improve diagnostic accuracy, while more studies are required before the adoption of digital pathology for the diagnosis of HPV-independent cervical carcinomas. Recognition of suspicious clinical features, liberal use of immunocytochemistry, and molecular testing are essential to accurate cytologic diagnosis of HPV-independent cervical carcinomas.

articles.title: Intravascular Optical Coherence Tomography for Neuroendovascular Intervention: Applications, Devices, and Future Directions.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Intravascular optical coherence tomography (OCT) is a near-infrared light-based imaging modality with an axial resolution approaching 10 µm, roughly tenfold finer than intravascular ultrasound. Although OCT is established in coronary practice, its use in the cerebral circulation has been limited by catheter crossing profile, vessel tortuosity, and the need to clear blood from the vascular lumen during acquisition. In this narrative review, we summarize the physical principles of OCT, its plaque-characterization criteria and their histologic validation, the coronary evidence base, the imaging hardware available for intracranial use, and the reported clinical applications across intracranial atherosclerotic disease, intracranial aneurysms treated with flow diverters, carotid disease and carotid webs, arterial dissection, and venous and thromboembolic disease. We also discuss the technical barriers that limit routine neuroendovascular use. Methods: MEDLINE and PubMed were searched from inception through 1 September 2026 for English-language reports of intravascular OCT in human or animal cervical and intracranial vessels; study selection was not systematic. Results: The evidence base is composed largely of preclinical models, small human feasibility series, and case reports; no randomized or large-scale clinical outcome data exist. OCT has been feasible in selected cerebrovascular series, but the pooled evidence comes largely from extracranial carotid studies and does not establish its performance in intracranial vessels. Dedicated neurovascular probes have recently entered clinical study. In the coronary circulation, randomized evidence supports intravascular imaging-guided stent implantation and OCT-defined plaque features are associated with events; corresponding benefits have not been established intracranially. Conclusions: Intravascular OCT resolves the cerebral arterial wall and endoluminal devices in detail, but its safety and clinical benefit in neuroendovascular practice require further study. Prospective studies are needed to determine whether OCT findings change management and improve patient outcomes.

articles.title: Convolutional Neural Network-Based Deep Learning Models for Diagnosis of Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma and Oral Potentially Malignant Disorders: A Scoping Review.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) represents the most common oral malignancy, accounting for over 90% of cases, with a five-year survival rate of approximately 50%. Oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs) carry an inherent risk of malignant transformation to OSCC, yet early and accurate diagnosis of both conditions remains challenging in clinical practice, owing to lesion heterogeneity and inter-observer variability in histopathological interpretation. While existing reviews have addressed artificial intelligence (AI) models' diagnostic performance in oral oncology, these have typically combined varied model types and have not restricted inclusion to studies based on a held-out test set. This scoping review maps convolutional neural network (CNN)-based models applied with explicit diagnostic intent primarily to OSCC, with exploratory coverage of OPMDs, across histopathological and clinical photographic imaging, limited to studies reporting performance on held-out test data separate from model development. Methods: Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, a systematic search was conducted in August 2025 across Scopus, PubMed, and the Cochrane Library. Studies were included if they applied CNN-based models with explicit diagnostic intent for OPMDs and/or OSCC using histopathological or clinical photographic images and reported quantitative diagnostic performance on a held-out test set. Extracted data included model architecture, imaging modality, dataset characteristics, and performance metrics comprising accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve). Results: Thirty studies published between 2020 and 2025 were included. CNN-based models reported generally favorable diagnostic performance, particularly with histopathological images, with accuracy frequently exceeding 90%. Models utilizing clinical photographic images demonstrated greater variability, with accuracy ranging from approximately 76% to 97.5%, in the seven of 13 studies that reported it. Across both modalities, binary classification tasks generally outperformed multi-class differentiation. Inconsistent metric reporting, reliance on small single-institution datasets, and near-absent reporting of external validation were observed as recurring methodological limitations. Conclusions: CNN-based models reported high diagnostic performance for OSCC, particularly in histopathological binary classification settings, although evidence for OPMD subtypes remains limited. However, translating this into clinical practice will require investment in large shared data repositories, standardized reporting of performance metrics, rigorous benchmarking against human experts, and external and prospective clinical validation.

articles.title: Semiquantitative 99mTc-MIBI Thyroid Uptake in Amiodarone-Induced Thyrotoxicosis: A Single-Centre Observational Imaging Study.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Differentiating amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis (AIT) types remains challenging because clinical, biochemical, and imaging findings frequently overlap. This study evaluated semiquantitative technetium-99m methoxyisobutylisonitrile (MIBI) thyroid uptake using a mediastinal background region to characterize the distribution of thyroid uptake patterns in patients with AIT. Methods: In this single-centre observational study, 55 patients with AIT and 35 euthyroid controls underwent early and delayed planar MIBI thyroid scintigraphy. Semiquantitative analysis was performed using thyroid-to-background ratios (TBR). Patients were stratified into exploratory low-, intermediate-, and high-uptake groups according to TBR tertiles. Early and delayed TBR measurements, their association, and stability of relative uptake grouping were analyzed. Laboratory parameters, thyroid ultrasound, and 99mTc-pertechnetate scintigraphy were evaluated as complementary diagnostic tools.
